Explanation: Each blocks platelet ADP signaling through P2Y12, reducing platelet activation and aggregation.
Source Section: Platelets - Antiplatelet Medications; PDF p. 51
Notes: All four are P2Y12/ADP-receptor antagonists. Clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticlopidine are thienopyridine prodrugs; ticagrelor is a direct, reversible non-thienopyridine. Do not call all four irreversible. Ticlopidine is legacy (neutropenia/TTP). Ref: Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 14th ed.

Explanation: These four numbered coagulation factors require vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation for normal function.
Source Section: Coagulation and Fibrinolysis - Vitamin K; PDF p. 61
Notes: Verified. Proteins C and S are also vitamin K-dependent but are anticoagulants; the procoagulant-factor title correctly excludes them. Board overlap: avoid pairing with a separate 'vitamin K-dependent protein' group on the same board. Ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed.

Connection Title: Intrinsic-pathway factors in the classic cascade
Explanation: These factors participate in the traditional intrinsic coagulation cascade assessed by aPTT.
Source Section: Coagulation and Fibrinolysis - Coagulation Cascade; PDF p. 54
Notes: Verified classic laboratory cascade. Factor XII deficiency prolongs aPTT without a bleeding phenotype. Factor IX overlaps with the vitamin K-dependent set (PLX-HEM-002); separate the two on a board. Ref: Hoffman Hematology: Basic Principles and Practice, 8th ed.

Explanation: Each is associated with cold-reactive antibodies that can cause immune hemolysis, often through complement activation.
Source Section: Normocytic Anemia - Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia; PDF p. 34
Notes: Verified: Mycoplasma and EBV cause infection-associated cold agglutinin syndrome; Waldenstrom/LPL and CLL/other B-cell lymphoproliferations cause secondary cold agglutinin syndrome. CLL more classically causes warm AIHA, so flag board overlap with a warm-AIHA group. Distinguish primary cold agglutinin disease from secondary syndrome. Refs: Berentsen & Barcellini, Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemias, N Engl J Med 2021; Berentsen, Curr Oncol Rep 2024.

Connection Title: Drugs associated with immune hemolytic anemia
Explanation: These drugs can cause immune-mediated red-cell destruction through differing antibody mechanisms.
Source Section: Normocytic Anemia - Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia; PDF p. 34
Notes: Verified. Mechanisms differ (hapten/drug-adsorption for penicillin/cephalosporins; immune-complex for rifampin/cephalosporins; autoantibody/warm-type for methyldopa). Tiles mix a class and named drugs, matching source granularity; do not imply a single shared mechanism. Ref: Garratty G, Blood 2010;115(2):168-9; Robbins 10th ed.

Explanation: These exposures or illnesses can increase oxidative stress and precipitate hemolysis in susceptible people with G6PD deficiency.
Source Section: Normocytic Anemia - G6PD Deficiency; PDF p. 32
Notes: Verified. Risk is drug- and dose-specific (e.g., primaquine/dapsone higher risk); not every antimalarial or sulfonamide is equally hemolytic. Infection is a common endogenous oxidative trigger. Preserve 'can precipitate' wording. Ref: Luzzatto L, Blood 2020;136(11):1225-1240.

Explanation: Oxidant injury in G6PD deficiency produces denatured hemoglobin and splenic removal of damaged portions of red cells; the disorder is classically X-linked recessive.
Source Section: Normocytic Anemia - G6PD Deficiency; PDF p. 32
Notes: Verified. Heinz bodies and bite cells occur in other oxidative hemolytic states; the four-member set is specific when combined. Ref: Luzzatto L, Blood 2020;136(11):1225-1240; Robbins 10th ed.

Explanation: Membrane loss produces spherical red cells with reduced surface-area-to-volume ratio. Increased MCHC and fragility with a negative antiglobulin test favor hereditary spherocytosis.
Source Section: Normocytic Anemia - Hereditary Spherocytosis; PDF p. 31
Notes: Verified. Spherocytes with a POSITIVE DAT indicate warm AIHA; the negative-DAT tile is the key discriminator, so keep it. EMA-binding and acidified glycerol lysis are modern confirmatory tests. Ref: Bolton-Maggs PHB et al., Br J Haematol 2012 (BCSH guideline).

Explanation: An acquired stem-cell PIGA defect reduces GPI-anchored complement regulators and creates a syndrome of hemolysis and thrombosis.
Source Section: Normocytic Anemia - Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria; PDF p. 30
Notes: Verified. PIGA is somatically ACQUIRED (not inherited). Thrombosis and cytopenias need not occur in every patient; diagnosis is by flow cytometry (CD55/CD59, FLAER). Ref: Brodsky RA, Blood 2014;124(18):2804-2811.

Explanation: Red-cell destruction releases LDH and hemoglobin and increases bilirubin generation; functioning marrow usually compensates with increased reticulocytes.
Source Section: Normocytic Anemia - Hemolysis; PDF p. 28
Notes: Verified. Reticulocytosis may be absent with concurrent marrow suppression, aplastic crisis, or nutrient deficiency; haptoglobin is more reliably low in intravascular than extravascular hemolysis. Preserve 'usually'. Ref: Robbins 10th ed.; Hoffman 8th ed.

Explanation: Each can mechanically fragment red cells and produce schistocytes on the peripheral smear.
Source Section: Normocytic Anemia - Additional Causes; PDF p. 37; Platelets p. 50; Coagulation p. 60
Notes: Verified. TTP/HUS/DIC are microangiopathic; prosthetic-valve hemolysis is macroangiopathic. Do not title this group exclusively 'microangiopathic hemolytic anemia'. Board overlap with dedicated TTP (PLX-HEM-034), HUS (035) and DIC (040) groups. Ref: George JN & Nester CM, N Engl J Med 2014;371(7):654-666.

Explanation: Sickling and microvascular obstruction contribute to these recognized manifestations of sickle cell disease.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Vaso-occlusive complications of sickle cell disease
Source Section: Normocytic Anemia - Sickle Cell Anemia; PDF p. 29
Notes: Verified. Acute chest syndrome is multifactorial (infection, fat embolism, infarction); do not imply a single mechanism per episode. Ref: Piel FB, Steinberg MH, Rees DC, N Engl J Med 2017;376(16):1561-1573.

Explanation: Sickling changes red-cell morphology, chronic hemolysis stimulates reticulocytes, and functional asplenia allows nuclear remnants to persist.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Peripheral blood findings in sickle cell disease
Source Section: Normocytic Anemia - Sickle Cell Anemia; PDF p. 29
Notes: Verified. Howell-Jolly bodies require functional asplenia/autosplenectomy (stage-dependent); reticulocytes fall during parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis. Target cells overlap with thalassemia/liver disease. Ref: Piel FB et al., N Engl J Med 2017;376(16):1561-1573.

Explanation: An inherited glycolytic defect reduces red-cell ATP, impairing membrane homeostasis and promoting splenic destruction; echinocytes may be seen.
Source Section: Normocytic Anemia - Pyruvate Kinase Deficiency; PDF p. 33
Notes: Verified. PKLR-associated autosomal recessive disorder; echinocytes are non-specific and may be absent (preserve 'may be seen'). Ref: Grace RF, Barcellini W, Blood 2020;136(11):1241-1249.

Explanation: Depleted stores with increased iron-binding capacity and reduced circulating iron form the classic uncomplicated iron-deficiency pattern; transferrin saturation (serum iron divided by TIBC) is low.
Source Section: Microcytic Anemia - Iron Deficiency Anemia; PDF p. 18
Notes: CORRECTION: original tiles paired 'High transferrin' and 'High TIBC', which measure essentially the same quantity (TIBC closely tracks serum transferrin) and are not distinct tiles. Replaced 'High transferrin' with 'Low transferrin saturation' (TSAT <16-20% in iron deficiency) to give four distinct parameters. Inflammation can raise ferritin and mask the pattern. Refs: Auerbach M & DeLoughery TG, Iron Deficiency in Adults: A Review, JAMA 2025; Rohr M et al., Eur J Med Res 2023;28(1):15.

Explanation: These clinical findings or syndromic associations are recognized in iron deficiency, although none must be present.
Source Section: Microcytic Anemia - Iron Deficiency Anemia; PDF p. 18
Notes: Verified. Glossitis is shared with B12/folate deficiency; Plummer-Vinson is a syndrome that CONTAINS iron deficiency (plus esophageal web, dysphagia) rather than a symptom. Preserve 'none must be present'. Ref: Auerbach M & DeLoughery TG, JAMA 2025; Robbins 10th ed.

Explanation: Each can cause sustained blood loss and eventual depletion of iron stores.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Chronic blood loss causing iron deficiency
Source Section: Microcytic Anemia - Iron Deficiency Anemia; PDF p. 18
Notes: Verified. Retain 'bleeding' qualifiers; non-bleeding ulcers/tumors do not cause iron deficiency. Hookworm (Ancylostoma/Necator) is a leading global cause. Ref: Camaschella C, N Engl J Med 2015;372(19):1832-1843.

Explanation: Inflammatory signaling increases hepcidin and sequesters iron while reducing transferrin, producing low available iron despite retained stores.
Source Section: Microcytic Anemia - Anemia of Chronic Disease; PDF p. 19
Notes: Verified. Concurrent iron deficiency can lower ferritin into the normal range; the anemia is often normocytic rather than microcytic. Contrast directly with the iron-deficiency pattern (PLX-HEM-015). Ref: Weiss G, Ganz T, Goodnough LT, Blood 2019;133(1):40-50.

Explanation: Lead exposure can affect peripheral nerves, the gastrointestinal tract, gingiva, and cognition.
Source Section: Microcytic Anemia - Lead Toxicity; PDF p. 20
Notes: Verified. Motor neuropathy/wrist drop is more typical in adults; encephalopathy and cognitive effects dominate in children. These are possible, not simultaneous, features. Ref: CDC/ATSDR Lead Toxicity resource; Robbins 10th ed.

Explanation: Lead disrupts heme synthesis at two enzyme steps and can impair red-cell RNA degradation, producing these biochemical and smear findings.
Source Section: Microcytic Anemia - Lead Toxicity; PDF p. 20
Notes: Verified. Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase; basophilic stippling (impaired pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase) is non-specific; blood lead level is diagnostic. Ref: ATSDR Toxicological Profile for Lead; Robbins 10th ed.

Explanation: Each exposure is associated with acquired sideroblastic anemia, through differing effects on heme synthesis or mitochondrial function.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Drug and toxin causes of sideroblastic anemia
Source Section: Microcytic Anemia - Sideroblastic Anemia; PDF p. 21
Notes: Verified independently: all four cause acquired sideroblastic anemia. Isoniazid acts via B6/pyridoxine antagonism; alcohol, chloramphenicol and linezolid impair mitochondrial function/protein synthesis. Do NOT state all four cause B6 depletion. Refs: Patnaik MM & Tefferi A, Am J Hematol 2017;92(3):297-310; Linezolid US FDA label (sideroblastic anemia, Adverse Reactions).

Explanation: Impaired incorporation of iron into heme produces mitochondrial iron accumulation and an iron-rich laboratory pattern.
Source Section: Microcytic Anemia - Sideroblastic Anemia; PDF p. 21
Notes: Verified. MCV varies by etiology (congenital often microcytic; acquired/MDS often normo-macrocytic) - do not require microcytosis. Ring sideroblasts also define MDS-RS. Ref: Patnaik MM & Tefferi A, Am J Hematol 2017;92(3):297-310.

Explanation: These correspond to loss or severe inactivation of one, two, three, and four alpha-globin genes in the classic deletion model.
Source Section: Microcytic Anemia - Alpha-Thalassemia; PDF p. 23
Notes: Verified 1-/2-/3-/4-gene deletion series. Nondeletional variants exist; rare four-gene (Hb Bart) survival has been reported with intrauterine transfusion, so avoid the absolute 'always incompatible with life' phrasing. Ref: Taher AT, Musallam KM, Cappellini MD, N Engl J Med 2021;384(8):727-743.

Explanation: Reduced beta-globin synthesis shifts hemoglobin fractions and causes ineffective erythropoiesis with characteristic morphology and skeletal effects in severe disease.
Source Section: Microcytic Anemia - Beta-Thalassemia; PDF p. 24
Notes: Verified. HbF is markedly elevated; HbA2 is usually elevated but may be variable by genotype/transfusion and is the hallmark of beta-thalassemia TRAIT - keep qualifier. 'Crew-cut' skull and chipmunk facies reflect marrow expansion. Ref: Taher AT et al., N Engl J Med 2021;384(8):727-743.

Explanation: Loss of intrinsic factor, loss of the ileal absorption site, or impaired pancreatic processing can interfere with B12 absorption.
Source Section: Macrocytic Anemia - Cobalamin Deficiency; PDF p. 42
Notes: Verified. Each targets a distinct step (IF production, gastric source, ileal receptor site, pancreatic protease release of B12 from R-binder). Deficiency risk depends on extent of surgery/dysfunction. Ref: Stabler SP, N Engl J Med 2013;368(2):149-160.

Explanation: B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and B12-dependent metabolic reactions and can injure spinal cord tracts.
Source Section: Macrocytic Anemia - Cobalamin Deficiency; PDF p. 42
Notes: Verified. Elevated MMA distinguishes B12 from folate deficiency (board overlap with PLX-HEM-028); neuro and hematologic findings can occur independently. Renal impairment can raise MMA. Ref: Stabler SP, N Engl J Med 2013;368(2):149-160.

Explanation: Increased demand, inadequate intake, or drug-associated interference can reduce available folate and predispose to megaloblastic anemia.
Source Section: Macrocytic Anemia - Folate Deficiency; PDF p. 41
Notes: Verified as risk factors/contexts (not diagnoses). Pregnancy = increased demand; supplementation modifies risk. Phenytoin impairs folate absorption/metabolism. Ref: Green R, Blood 2017;129(19):2603-2611.

Explanation: Folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and homocysteine metabolism without directly disrupting the B12-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA pathway.
Source Section: Macrocytic Anemia - Folate Deficiency; PDF p. 41
Notes: Verified. Normal MMA with elevated homocysteine is the key folate-vs-B12 discriminator (board overlap with PLX-HEM-026). Megaloblastic morphology and hypersegmentation are shared with B12 deficiency. Ref: Green R, Blood 2017;129(19):2603-2611.

Explanation: A defect in de novo pyrimidine synthesis raises orotate and impairs DNA synthesis while leaving the urea cycle intact.
Source Section: Macrocytic Anemia - Orotic Aciduria; PDF p. 43
Notes: Verified. Normal ammonia distinguishes hereditary orotic aciduria from ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency (which has high orotic acid AND hyperammonemia). Treat with uridine. Ref: Bailey CJ, J Inherit Metab Dis 2009;32(2):227-233.

Explanation: Congenital erythroid failure produces an infantile macrocytic anemia with poor reticulocyte production and possible developmental anomalies.
Source Section: Macrocytic Anemia - Non-Megaloblastic Anemia; PDF p. 44
Notes: Verified. Ribosomopathy (e.g., RPS19). Congenital anomalies (triphalangeal thumb, craniofacial) occur in a subset only; HbF and adenosine deaminase activity are often elevated. Distinguish from transient erythroblastopenia of childhood. Ref: Da Costa L et al., Blood 2020;136(11):1262-1273.

Explanation: These are stored in platelet dense (delta) granules and contribute to platelet activation or local vascular responses after release.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Platelet delta-granule contents; dense granule contents
Source Section: Platelets - Overview; PDF p. 47
Notes: CORRECTION: replaced 'Histamine' with 'ATP'. Authoritative sources list dense/delta-granule contents as ADP, ATP, serotonin (5-HT), calcium (and zinc); histamine is characteristically a mast-cell/basophil granule product, not a canonical platelet dense-granule constituent. Board overlap: keep separate from any alpha-granule content group (fibrinogen, vWF, PDGF, P-selectin). Refs: Holinstat M, Cancer Metastasis Rev 2017;36(2):195-198; Yao HHY & Kahr WHA, J Thromb Haemost 2025 (PMID 39617187); Cooper C & Halligan K, Pediatr Rev 2025.

Explanation: Defective platelet adhesion, aggregation, platelet survival, or vWF function can produce mucocutaneous bleeding.
Source Section: Platelets - Platelet Disorders; PDF p. 49; Coagulation - vWD p. 58
Notes: Verified. BSS = GPIb-IX-V adhesion defect (often with thrombocytopenia/large platelets); Glanzmann = GPIIb/IIIa aggregation defect; ITP = reduced platelet survival; vWD = adhesion defect that can also lower factor VIII (secondary hemostasis). Avoid a 'normal platelet count' qualifier in the title. Ref: Robbins 10th ed.; Leebeek FWG & Eikenboom JCJ, N Engl J Med 2016;375(21):2067-2080.

Explanation: These approaches reduce immune platelet destruction or increase platelet production in selected patients with ITP.
Source Section: Platelets - Immune Thrombocytopenia; PDF p. 49
Notes: Verified. First-line = corticosteroids +/- IVIG; rituximab and TPO-receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim, avatrombopag) are second-line. Not an interchangeable or fixed sequence; selection depends on severity/bleeding/chronicity. Ref: Neunert C et al., ASH 2019 ITP guidelines, Blood Adv 2019;3(23):3829-3866.

Explanation: Deficient cleavage of vWF multimers permits platelet-rich microthrombi, consuming platelets and fragmenting red cells.
Source Section: Platelets - Thrombotic Microangiopathies; PDF p. 50
Notes: Verified. ADAMTS13 activity typically <10%. Not all thrombotic microangiopathies are TTP; the historic pentad is not required for diagnosis. Board overlap with schistocyte group (PLX-HEM-011) and HUS (035). Ref: Joly BS, Coppo P, Veyradier A, Blood 2017;129(21):2836-2846.

Explanation: Shiga-toxin endothelial injury can produce a postdiarrheal thrombotic microangiopathy with prominent renal dysfunction.
Source Section: Platelets - Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome; PDF p. 50
Notes: Verified. Diarrhea (E. coli O157:H7/Shiga toxin) is a prodrome, usually but not invariably bloody. Title correctly excludes complement-mediated (atypical) HUS. Board overlap with TTP (034). Ref: Fakhouri F et al., Lancet 2017;390(10095):681-696.

Explanation: Impaired vWF function affects platelet adhesion and can lower factor VIII, with a generally normal PT and variable aPTT.
Source Section: Coagulation and Fibrinolysis - Von Willebrand Disease; PDF p. 58
Notes: Verified. aPTT prolongs only when factor VIII is sufficiently reduced; platelet count falls in type 2B. Ristocetin cofactor activity/behavior varies by subtype - keep qualifiers. Ref: Leebeek FWG & Eikenboom JCJ, N Engl J Med 2016;375(21):2067-2080.

Explanation: Reduced anticoagulant activity, resistance to activated protein C, or increased prothrombin can promote inherited venous thrombosis.
Source Section: Coagulation and Fibrinolysis - Thrombophilia; PDF p. 57
Notes: Verified. Not exhaustive - protein S deficiency equally qualifies (board overlap/alternate member). Antithrombin and protein C deficiency can also be acquired. Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia. Ref: Connors JM, N Engl J Med 2017;377(12):1177-1187.

Explanation: The syndrome involves antiphospholipid antibodies; cross-reactivity can also produce a false-positive RPR or VDRL.
Source Section: Coagulation and Fibrinolysis - Thrombophilia; PDF p. 57
Notes: Verified. The three laboratory criteria antibodies plus the classic false-positive nontreponemal (VDRL/RPR) test; the latter is neither necessary nor a classification criterion. Diagnosis requires persistent antibody positivity (>=12 weeks) plus clinical events. Ref: Garcia D & Erkan D, N Engl J Med 2018;378(21):2010-2021.

Explanation: Reduced vitamin K-dependent factors, impaired hepatic synthesis, or factor consumption can prolong PT.
Source Section: Coagulation and Fibrinolysis - Hemostasis Diagnostics; PDF p. 55
Notes: Verified. PT reflects the extrinsic/common pathway (factor VII is shortest half-life); may be normal early. Each listed cause can also prolong aPTT at some stage. Ref: Hoffman 8th ed.; Robbins 10th ed.

Explanation: Consumption of platelets and coagulation factors with fibrin turnover produces this classic pattern of overt DIC.
Source Section: Coagulation and Fibrinolysis - DIC; PDF p. 60
Notes: Verified overt-DIC pattern. Fibrinogen (acute-phase reactant) may be normal/high early despite consumption; trend matters. Ref: Levi M & Scully M, Blood 2018;131(8):845-854.

Explanation: These locations contribute to red-cell production at different stages of prenatal development, with marrow later becoming dominant.
Source Section: Embryology - Fetal Erythropoiesis; PDF p. 3
Notes: Verified (mnemonic 'Young Liver Synthesizes Blood': Yolk sac -> Liver -> Spleen -> Bone marrow). Sites overlap in time; treat gestational cutoffs as approximate. Ref: Sadler TW, Langman's Medical Embryology, 14th ed.

Explanation: These infections can produce necrotizing or caseating granulomatous inflammation in an appropriate host and tissue context.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Necrotizing granuloma infections; caseating granuloma infections
Source Section: Principles of Oncology and Therapeutics - Necrosis; PDF p. 68
Notes: Original ambiguity 2 downgraded to 1 after independent verification. Title clarified to 'caseating/necrotizing'. Cryptococcosis DOES cause necrotizing or non-necrotizing granulomas in immunocompetent hosts but frequently shows little/no granulomatous reaction (mucoid/gelatinous lesions) in immunocompromised hosts - keep the host qualifier. BOARD OVERLAP WARNING: blastomycosis is an equally strong (arguably cleaner) alternate member; if a competing 'endemic mycosis' tile set is on the board, prefer swapping cryptococcosis for blastomycosis to avoid dispute. Ref: El-Zammar OA & Katzenstein AL, Histopathology 2007;50(3):289-310.

Explanation: These tumors can contain concentrically laminated calcific bodies called psammoma bodies.
Source Section: Principles of Oncology and Therapeutics - Calcification; PDF p. 69
Notes: Verified classic 'PSaMMoma' set (Papillary thyroid, Serous ovarian, Meningioma, Mesothelioma). Frequency differs: common in papillary thyroid and serous ovarian/meningioma, present but less prominent in epithelioid mesothelioma. Prolactinoma and papillary lung/renal adenocarcinoma are rarer associations. Refs: Braun A et al., Diagn Cytopathol 2024; Beasley MB et al., Virchows Arch 2021 (mesothelioma).

Explanation: These agents interfere with purine-related nucleic-acid metabolism or synthesis; their activation pathways and clinical indications differ.
Source Section: Principles of Oncology and Therapeutics - Drug Targets; PDF p. 73
Notes: Verified. Azathioprine is a prodrug of 6-MP (thiopurines; TPMT-dependent). Cladribine and fludarabine are purine nucleoside analogues used in hairy cell leukemia/CLL. Cladribine is not strictly S-phase/cell-cycle specific - avoid that blanket label. Ref: Goodman & Gilman's, 14th ed.

Explanation: These pyrimidine-related antimetabolites interfere with nucleic-acid synthesis; capecitabine is converted to 5-fluorouracil.
Source Section: Principles of Oncology and Therapeutics - Drug Targets; PDF p. 73
Notes: Verified. Capecitabine is the oral prodrug of 5-FU (distinct drugs, acceptable as separate tiles). Mechanisms differ: 5-FU/capecitabine inhibit thymidylate synthase; cytarabine/gemcitabine are incorporated as fraudulent nucleotides and inhibit DNA polymerase/ribonucleotide reductase. Do not claim all directly inhibit thymidylate synthase. Ref: Goodman & Gilman's, 14th ed.

Explanation: Irinotecan and topotecan target topoisomerase I; etoposide and teniposide target topoisomerase II.
Source Section: Principles of Oncology and Therapeutics - Drug Targets; PDF p. 73
Notes: CORRECTION: Discipline changed from Pathology to Pharmacology (chemotherapeutic drug group). Content verified: camptothecins (irinotecan/topotecan) inhibit topoisomerase I; epipodophyllotoxins (etoposide/teniposide) inhibit topoisomerase II. The set deliberately spans both isoforms - a narrower 'topo-I' or 'topo-II only' title would be rejectable. Ref: Goodman & Gilman's, 14th ed.

Explanation: The first pair blocks PD-1 and the second pair blocks PD-L1, interrupting the inhibitory checkpoint interaction.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: PD-1 axis checkpoint inhibitors; PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors
Source Section: Principles of Oncology and Therapeutics - Drug Targets; PDF p. 74
Notes: Verified: pembrolizumab and nivolumab target PD-1; atezolizumab and durvalumab target PD-L1. Do NOT label all four anti-PD-1. Board overlap: ipilimumab (CTLA-4) and avelumab (PD-L1) are plausible distractors/alternates. Refs: Klempner SJ et al., JAMA 2025; Morad G et al., Cell 2021;184(21):5309-5337.

Explanation: These agents damage DNA through crosslink formation; cisplatin is a platinum compound that crosslinks DNA rather than a classic alkylating agent.
Source Section: Principles of Oncology and Therapeutics - Drug Targets; PDF p. 74
Notes: Verified. Busulfan (alkyl sulfonate), cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide (oxazaphosphorine nitrogen mustards) are classic alkylators; cisplatin forms platinum-DNA crosslinks ('alkylating-like'). Keep the class qualifier in the explanation. Pair with supportive agents in PLX-HEM-049 (mesna for oxazaphosphorines; amifostine for cisplatin). Ref: Goodman & Gilman's, 14th ed.

Connection Title: Supportive agents paired with cancer-drug toxicity
Explanation: These agents are paired, respectively, with protection from oxazaphosphorine (cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide) bladder toxicity, anthracycline cardiotoxicity, selected cisplatin toxicity, and methotrexate toxicity.
Source Section: Principles of Oncology and Therapeutics - Drug Targets; PDF pp. 73-74
Notes: Verified pairings: mesna (hemorrhagic cystitis), dexrazoxane (anthracycline cardioprotection), amifostine (cisplatin nephro-/neuro- and radiation toxicity), leucovorin (folinic acid rescue after high-dose methotrexate; also potentiates 5-FU). Roles differ; do not imply universal prophylaxis. Ref: Goodman & Gilman's, 14th ed.; NCCN supportive care references.

Explanation: These proteins or fusion products promote oncogenic signaling through tyrosine-kinase or serine/threonine-kinase activity.
Source Section: Principles of Oncology and Therapeutics - Oncogene table; PDF p. 72
Notes: Verified. Not all are receptor tyrosine kinases: HER2/ERBB2 is a receptor TK; BCR-ABL1 and JAK2 are non-receptor TKs; BRAF is a serine/threonine kinase. Keep the broad 'kinase' framing; a 'receptor tyrosine kinase' title would be rejectable. Ref: Weinberg RA, The Biology of Cancer, 2nd ed.

Explanation: Classic rearrangements involve MYC [t(8;14)], BCL2 [t(14;18)], CCND1/cyclin D1 [t(11;14)], and BIRC3-MALT1 [t(11;18)], respectively, in subsets of these lymphoid neoplasms.
Source Section: Leukemias and Lymphomas - B-cell Neoplasms; PDF p. 82
Notes: Verified independently. Gastric MALT lymphoma: t(11;18)(q21;q21) BIRC3-MALT1 (synonym API2-MALT1 / c-IAP2-MALT1), the most frequent translocation in gastric MALT (~21-40%). No translocation is universal within its disease. Refs: Rossi D, Bertoni F, Zucca E, Marginal-Zone Lymphomas, N Engl J Med 2022;386(6):568-581; Nakamura S et al., Gut 2007 (PMID 17525089).

Explanation: BCR-ABL1-driven granulocytic proliferation produces the classic CML laboratory and smear pattern.
Source Section: Leukemias and Lymphomas - CML; PDF p. 78
Notes: Verified. Low LAP/NAP score is a traditional clue (distinguishes CML from leukemoid reaction) but is not the confirmatory test; BCR-ABL1 by FISH/PCR confirms. BCR-ABL1 also occurs in Ph+ ALL; the full set favors CML. Ref: Hehlmann R, N Engl J Med 2020;383(14):1358-1366 (CML review).

Explanation: PML-RARA disrupts myeloid differentiation; the classic subtype has abnormal promyelocytes that may contain Auer rods and responds to differentiation therapy.
Source Section: Leukemias and Lymphomas - AML and APL; PDF p. 77
Notes: CORRECTION: cytogenetic tile notation fixed from 't(15,17)' to the standard 't(15;17)' (semicolon separates the two chromosomes). Content verified: t(15;17)(q24;q21) PML-RARA; faggot cells/Auer rods; sensitivity to ATRA +/- arsenic trioxide; risk of DIC. Rare variant RARA fusions can be ATRA-resistant. Ref: Robbins 10th ed.; Sanz MA et al., Blood 2019;133(15):1630-1643.

Explanation: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma typically shows characteristic malignant cells, this immunophenotype, and an orderly lymph-node spread pattern.
Source Section: Leukemias and Lymphomas - Hodgkin Lymphoma; PDF p. 81
Notes: Verified. Classical HL Reed-Sternberg cells are CD15+/CD30+ (CD45-, usually CD20-); CD15 can be absent in a minority. Contiguous nodal spread is typical, not mandatory. Title correctly excludes nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL (CD20+, CD15-/CD30-, LP 'popcorn' cells). Ref: Ansell SM, N Engl J Med 2021 (Hodgkin lymphoma review).

Explanation: MYC-driven proliferation produces an aggressive lymphoma with classic histology and different common anatomic presentations by epidemiologic form.
Source Section: Leukemias and Lymphomas - Burkitt Lymphoma; PDF p. 82
Notes: Verified. t(8;14) MYC-IGH; 'starry-sky' = tingible-body macrophages amid high-turnover tumor (non-specific); endemic (African, EBV, jaw) vs sporadic (abdominal/ileocecal) forms are distinct presentations not required together. Board overlap with MYC tile in PLX-HEM-051 - do not place both on one board. Ref: Robbins 10th ed.

Explanation: Classic hairy cell leukemia has characteristic morphology and molecular or cytochemical features, with marrow fibrosis that can impede aspiration.
Source Section: Leukemias and Lymphomas - Hairy Cell Leukemia; PDF p. 82
Notes: Verified. BRAF V600E is characteristic of classic HCL; HCL-variant typically lacks it and differs in markers - keep 'classic' qualifier. Dry tap from reticulin fibrosis is common, not universal; immunophenotype CD11c/CD25/CD103/CD123+. Ref: Troussard X & Cornet E, Am J Hematol 2017;92(12):1382-1390.

Explanation: CLL involves a mature clonal lymphocyte population, fragile cells on smear, and risks of immune cytopenias and transformation to aggressive lymphoma.
Source Section: Leukemias and Lymphomas - CLL; PDF p. 80
Notes: Verified. Smudge (basket) cells are non-specific; AIHA (usually warm) and Richter transformation to DLBCL occur in a subset only, not as obligatory stages. Board overlap: CLL also appears in cold-agglutinin set (PLX-HEM-004). Ref: Hallek M, Al-Sawaf O, Am J Hematol 2021;96(12):1679-1705.

Explanation: This leukemic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma can produce widespread erythema, blood involvement, and characteristic malignant lymphocyte morphology.
Source Section: Leukemias and Lymphomas - Sezary Syndrome; PDF p. 83
Notes: Verified. Leukemic variant of CTCL: erythroderma + Sezary (cerebriform) cells + clonal blood CD4+ T cells (classically CD4+CD7-/CD26-) meeting defined blood tumor burden. Cerebriform nuclei alone are not diagnostic. Ref: Willemze R et al., Blood 2019;133(16):1703-1714 (WHO-EORTC classification).

Explanation: HTLV-1-associated mature T-cell malignancy can cause calcium elevation and bone or skin involvement.
Source Section: Leukemias and Lymphomas - Adult T-cell Lymphoma; PDF p. 83
Notes: Verified. ATLL is caused by HTLV-1; hypercalcemia (often with lytic lesions, PTHrP/RANKL-mediated) and skin involvement are characteristic but vary by clinical subtype (acute/lymphomatous/chronic/smoldering). Avoid implying all patients have acute disease. Ref: Cook LB et al., Blood 2021;137(4):459-470.

Explanation: Plasma-cell disease can cause bone destruction, light-chain renal injury, and marrow-related anemia, forming the CRAB pattern.
Source Section: Plasma Cell Dyscrasias - Multiple Myeloma; PDF p. 87
Notes: Verified. CRAB = hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lesions, attributable to the clonal plasma-cell disorder. Current IMWG criteria add myeloma-defining biomarkers (clonal marrow >=60%, FLC ratio >=100, >1 focal MRI lesion). Ref: Rajkumar SV, Am J Hematol 2022;97(8):1086-1107; IMWG criteria 2014.

Explanation: Monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains can be detected in serum or urine and can injure the kidney or deposit as amyloid.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Consequences and detection of monoclonal light chains
Source Section: Plasma Cell Dyscrasias - Multiple Myeloma; PDF p. 87
Notes: Verified. These are detection findings (Bence Jones/urine light chains, abnormal serum free light-chain ratio) and complications (cast nephropathy, AL amyloidosis) of monoclonal light chains - a mechanism-linked set rather than four diseases. AL amyloidosis does not require overt myeloma. Keep title emphasizing the shared pathogenic protein. Ref: Rajkumar SV, Am J Hematol 2022;97(8):1086-1107.

Explanation: An IgM-secreting lymphoplasmacytic malignancy can cause viscosity-related symptoms, neuropathy, and cold-antibody phenomena.
Source Section: Plasma Cell Dyscrasias - Waldenstrom Macroglobulinemia; PDF p. 88
Notes: Verified. Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with monoclonal IgM and frequent MYD88 L265P; hyperviscosity, IgM-related neuropathy (anti-MAG) and cold agglutinins occur in subsets, not all patients. Do not require a pure plasma-cell marrow. Board overlap with cold-agglutinin set (PLX-HEM-004). Ref: Gertz MA, Am J Hematol 2021;96(2):258-269.

Explanation: Autonomous myeloid proliferation produces erythrocytosis with suppressed EPO and can cause water-triggered itching and marrow expansion across myeloid lines.
Source Section: Myeloproliferative Disease - Polycythemia Vera; PDF p. 89
Notes: Verified. JAK2 V617F (or exon 12) present in ~95%+ of PV but also in ET/PMF; low EPO plus panmyelosis distinguishes primary polycythemia from secondary. Aquagenic pruritus is characteristic. Ref: Spivak JL, N Engl J Med 2017;376(22):2168-2181.

Explanation: Fibrotic marrow and extramedullary hematopoiesis yield teardrop cells, a leukoerythroblastic smear (immature myeloid and nucleated red cells), and marked splenic enlargement.
Source Section: Myeloproliferative Disease - Myelofibrosis; PDF p. 90
Notes: Verified. 'Leukoerythroblastic' = circulating immature granulocytes plus nucleated RBCs, consistent with the source's nucleated-RBC/leukocytosis description. Dacrocytes (teardrop cells) and dry tap are typical; findings vary by stage and overlap other marrow-infiltrative disorders. JAK2/CALR/MPL driver mutations. Ref: Tefferi A, Am J Hematol 2021;96(1):145-162.

Explanation: Cell breakdown releases potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids; urate rises and phosphate binding can lower serum calcium.
Source Section: Myeloproliferative Disease - Tumor Lysis Syndrome; PDF p. 91
Notes: Verified Cairo-Bishop pattern: hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, secondary hypocalcemia. Abnormalities need not occur simultaneously; renal function and prophylaxis (hydration, allopurinol/rasburicase) modify severity. Ref: Howard SC, Jones DP, Pui CH, N Engl J Med 2011;364(19):1844-1854.
